### Problem: Longest Consecutive Sequence {#sec-hash-p5-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Given unsorted $a$ ($0 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9$, duplicates allowed), return the length of the longest run of **consecutive integers** present in $a$ (values, not positions — $[1, 9, 3, 10, 4, 20, 2]$ has the run $1,2,3,4$ of length $4$). Must be $O(n)$.

Source: [LC 128 · Longest Consecutive Sequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-consecutive-sequence/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Consecutive" is a statement about *values*, so sorting feels inevitable — but the required $O(n)$ forbids it, and a hash set gives the better primitive: with $s = \text{set}(a)$ you can ask "does $x-1$ exist?" instantly. Only **run starts** matter — values $x$ with no $x-1$ in $s$. Every value belongs to exactly one run and is stepped over by exactly one walk, the one that starts at the bottom of its run, so all the walks together take $O(n)$ steps even though a single walk can be long (@fig-hash-anim-runs).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Sort and count ascending runs.** Deduplicate with `sorted(set(a))`, then one scan counting streaks where the value increases by exactly $1$. $O(n\log n)$ — correct, and the honesty baseline for the stress loop.
2. **Set, extend only from starts.** $s = \text{set}(a)$; for each $x \in s$ *with $x - 1 \notin s$*, walk $x+1, x+2, \dots$ while inside $s$; keep the longest walk. $O(n)$ expected.

**Invariant.** When a walk from start $x$ finishes at $y$, every value of $[x, y]$ has now been counted toward that run and will never be walked again — the sets $\{x : x-1 \notin s\}$ partition $s$ into runs.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sort and count ascending runs

::: {.form-next}
Sorting puts consecutive values next to each other, which turns the value question back into an index question: scan the deduplicated sorted list, a run continues while `s[i] == s[i-1] + 1`, otherwise resets. $O(n\log n)$ — fine to write in an interview while you argue for form 2.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def longest_sort(a):
    s = sorted(set(a))
    if not s:
        return 0
    best = run = 1
    for i in range(1, len(s)):
        run = run + 1 if s[i] == s[i - 1] + 1 else 1
        best = max(best, run)
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int longestConsecutiveSort(vector<int> a) {       // by value: we rewrite it
    if (a.empty()) return 0;
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    a.erase(unique(a.begin(), a.end()), a.end()); // dedup: runs are over VALUES
    int best = 1, run = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        run = (a[i] == a[i - 1] + 1) ? run + 1 : 1;
        best = max(best, run);
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Set it, then walk only from the bottom

::: {.form-next}
Drop the sort for a set and the question "am I a run start?" becomes one lookup: $x - 1 \notin s$. Walk upward from each start only; the amortisation is the interview's whole point — every element is walked exactly once across all starts, so total work is $O(n)$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("longest", "starts")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-longest-consecutive
def longest_consecutive(a):
    s = set(a)
    best = 0
    for x in s:
        if x - 1 in s:
            continue                      # not a start - someone else counts it
        y = x + 1
        while y in s:
            y += 1                        # one-time cost, amortised over the run
        best = max(best, y - x)
    return best


for _ in range(2000):
    a = [random.randint(-3, 6) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))]
    assert longest_consecutive(a) == longest_sort(a)

assert longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]) == 4      # the LC examples
assert longest_consecutive([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1]) == 9
assert longest_consecutive([]) == 0
assert longest_consecutive([1, 1, 1]) == 1                   # duplicates collapse
assert longest_consecutive([-2, -1, 0, 5]) == 3              # negatives
print("longest_consecutive OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; cin >> n;
    unordered_set<long long> s;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { long long x; cin >> x; s.insert(x); }
    int best = 0;
    for (long long x : s) {
        if (s.count(x - 1)) continue;         // only run starts pay a walk
        long long y = x + 1;
        while (s.count(y)) ++y;
        best = max(best, (int)(y - x));
    }
    cout << best << '\n';
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Sort and count ascending runs** is $O(n\log n)$ guaranteed time, $O(n)$ space (in place on a copy). **Set it, then walk only from the bottom** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space — the walks share the work, because each value is stepped over by one walk only. The worst case is $\Theta(n^2)$ only if an adversary makes your set's keys collide (@sec-hash-anti), which matters on judges with hacks, not on LeetCode.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 0$: answer $0$ — the empty set makes the outer loop vanish; guard the sorted form's `s[0]` read.
- Duplicates: the set *is* the deduplication; the sorted form must `unique` explicitly — forgetting it breaks `run` continuity at equal neighbours.
- All one run: the walk is $O(n)$ once, $O(1)$ for every other element (all skip as non-starts).
- Values near $\pm 10^9$: $x - 1$ and $y + 1$ stay well inside the `int` range here, but the listing uses `long long` so the same code is safe when values reach the `int` limits (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1676F · Longest Strike](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1676/F){rating="1300"} — the longest run of consecutive values, counting only values that occur at least $k$ times.
- [CF 977F · Consecutive Subsequence](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/977/F){rating="1700"} — the run must also appear in index order: a map `best[x] = best[x - 1] + 1`, filled left to right, plus reconstruction.
:::
